## Analyst Notes

**STORY:** This is a heavily-loaded developer workstation for user `LABKA` (local admin `LABGALABGALABGALAB`) running a stack of AI coding assistants — Antigravity IDE, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex/ChatGPT, Docker Desktop, WSL — each maintaining active HTTPS 443 connections to Google, Anthropic (`api.anthropic.com` → `160.79.104.10`), and Cloudflare (`chatgpt.com` → `104.18.32.47`) infrastructure recorded in DNS cache. The two items that actually change the verdict are not the dev tooling itself but a scheduled task named **"SPLAT re-prove substrate"** with no author/path shown, and DNS cache entries **`splat2571c594ee9f4d2aa13651c4ff0bc2e2.192.0.2.1.nip.io`** / **`splat87710144bd564245bbc475c7cb69a800.192.0.2.1.nip.io`** — a dynamic-DNS (nip.io) pattern that resolves to the IP it encodes in its name, a classic low-cost C2/tunnelling technique. Both artifacts share the string "SPLAT," which is also this sensor's own codename — a coincidence worth treating with suspicion rather than dismissing as part of the diagnostic. A third decider: the enabled account `LABDALABDALABDALAB` has no recorded logon at all.

**KNOWN-GOOD:**
- `svchost.exe` listeners on 135/445/139/5357/49664-49682 owned by `services.exe`/`System` (PID 4) — standard Windows RPC/SMB stack, expected.
- `chrome.exe` (PID 27248, `C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\...`) talking to many Google/Cloudflare IPs including `142.251.15.188:5228` — Chrome's GCM push channel, expected on that port.
- `claude.exe` PID 9108 at `C:\Program Files\WindowsApps\Claude_2.19675.0.0_...` — Store-packaged, expected.
- **Lookalike that would NOT be waved through:** `claude.exe` at `C:\Users\LABKA\AppData\Roaming\Claude\claude-code\2.1.286\...` (PIDs 37152, 18464, 23512, 20872) — same product name, but unsigned and running from a user-writable AppData path with live established 443 connections. Meets the CRITICAL rule literally even though it is very plausibly the legitimate Claude Code CLI.
- `WidgetService.exe`, `MicrosoftStartFeedProvider.exe`, `IGCC.exe` show `NotSigned` but live under `C:\Program Files\WindowsApps\...` — expected Store/catalog signing behaviour, not escalated.
- Docker Desktop under `AppData\Local\Programs\DockerDesktop` is Docker's normal per-user install path — expected, not flagged as rogue despite "user-writable."

| Item | Benign explanation | Hostile explanation | Settles it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Antigravity/Claude/Codex unsigned AppData binaries w/ established conns | Normal self-updating AI IDE/CLI tools, distributed outside the Store | Trojanized or lookalike installer dropped in user profile | Hash/vendor-signature check against known release of Antigravity/Claude/Codex |
| Task "SPLAT re-prove substrate" | Some already-installed tool uses "SPLAT" as a product name coincidentally | Attacker-planted scheduled-task persistence (T1053.005) disguised to blend with this sensor's branding | `schtasks /query /tn "SPLAT re-prove substrate" /xml` for Action/binary path |
| DNS `splat*.192.0.2.1.nip.io` | Dev/test callback to a documentation IP (192.0.2.0/24 is RFC 5737 TEST-NET, non-routable) during tool testing | Dynamic-DNS C2 channel (T1568.002) | Correlate with a proxy/firewall log showing which process queried it and whether any TCP session to 192.0.2.1 occurred (none appears in the TCP table) |
| `svchost.exe` PID 5864 → `172.183.7.192:443`, no path shown | A normal Windows service (BITS/DoSvc) the sensor can't resolve a path for without admin rights | A malicious payload injected into a legitimate `svchost.exe` service host | `Get-Process -Id 5864 -IncludeUserName` / `Get-WmiObject Win32_Service` with elevated rights |
| `LABDALABDALABDALAB` enabled, no LastLogon | Sandbox account provisioned by Codex tooling but never used | Dormant backdoor account awaiting activation | Security event log 4624 for this SID — not visible from this sensor |

**PLAN:** 1) Cheap check first — pull the scheduled task XML for "SPLAT re-prove substrate" to see its binary path and trigger; this single fact either confirms a non-Microsoft user-writable-path persistence mechanism (escalate, contain) or reveals a benign vendor task. 2) Check whether anything actually opened a TCP session to `192.0.2.1` (none is in the current connection table) — if none, the DNS entry is likely a resolved-but-unused test artifact, downgrading urgency. 3) Resolve PIDs 6504/20516 (own established connections but absent from the process table — timing gap or hidden process) with a synchronized elevated snapshot. 4) Containment, if task/DNS correlate to a live process: isolate host from network, disable the task, kill the owning PID. 5) Cleanup — review `LABDALABDALABDALAB`, confirm local admin group is unchanged (`LABGALABGALABGALAB`, `Administrator` only), and get the unsigned AppData binaries hash-verified or allow-listed.

**Attack-chain note:** The evidence does not join into a complete chain. Persistence-stage evidence (T1053.005, the "SPLAT" task) and C2-stage evidence (T1568.002, the `splat*.nip.io` DNS entries) share a naming coincidence but no execution-stage or initial-access evidence links them, and no TCP connection in this capture actually reaches `192.0.2.1`. The single section that would turn this correlation into a confirmed chain is the **TCP connections table**: if it showed an established session from a process to `192.0.2.1:*` matching the DNS query time, that would tie persistence to live C2 and complete the picture.
